slides.h: If we lived inside a giant black hole, could we tell by looking at the sky?
b: One published model says the Big Bang was an explosion inside a black hole, with a shock-wave wall around everything we see.
If we're not at the exact center, shouldn't the sky look different in different directions? We computed the real answer.

slides.h: Two calculations, done blind — they agree to seven decimal places
b: I computed it this morning; a helper AI computed it overnight; neither saw the other's code.
When two independent calculations match that precisely, the math is almost certainly right.

slides.h: Inside the wall, everything looks perfectly normal — from anywhere
b: The interior is exactly a standard expanding universe, so measuring expansion in different directions can never reveal the wall.
We expected it could. The calculation says no. Our own idea got partially refuted — that is what honest math is for.

slides.h: The wall's only fingerprint: one round patch of strange sky
b: The wall shows up only if it is close enough that the cosmic microwave background sticks out past it — then you would see one big spot, tens of degrees wide, in one direction.

slides.h: No patch is seen — so the wall is either far and forever invisible, or barely at the edge
b: The microwave sky looks the same everywhere to one part in a hundred thousand.
The borderline case — where the known odd features of the largest-scale sky could be a patch's faint edge — is what we judge next.
